# Webinar Planning: Your Complete 2026 Guide to Flawless Virtual Events

by Paweł Łaniewski

November 28, 2025

Planning a webinar feels like juggling chainsaws while riding a unicycle, doesn’t it? You’re coordinating speakers, crafting promotional materials, testing technology, building landing pages, and somehow trying to ensure everything works perfectly when showtime arrives. Here’s the truth nobody tells you: about 90% of your webinar’s success is determined before you ever hit that “Go live” button.

The difference between a webinar that generates 85% attendance and drives real business results versus one where half your registrants ghost you? It’s not fancy camera equipment or professional lighting. It’s methodical, strategic planning that covers every detail from initial concept to post-event follow-up. Let’s dive into exactly how to plan a webinar that actually delivers results.

Table of Contents

Toggle

## Key Insights

- FAQ Section
- Success happens in preparation: The most effective webinars are built on comprehensive planning that addresses technical setup, audience engagement, promotional strategy, and contingency plans long before going live
- Automation saves events: Modern webinar platforms with automated reminders, follow-ups, and registration workflows reduce manual errors by up to 70% and dramatically improve attendance rates
- Engagement starts early: Interactive elements like polls, Q&A sessions, and chat features should be planned into your event structure from day one, not added as afterthoughts
- Technical rehearsals are non-negotiable: A complete run-through with all speakers, checking audio quality, screen sharing, and backup systems prevents 95% of live technical disasters
- Post-event strategy matters: Automated follow-up emails with recordings, certificates, and next-step CTAs can convert up to 40% more attendees into qualified leads
- Choose platforms for planning, not just streaming: The best webinar software excels at the entire event lifecycle—registration, branding, automation, and analytics—not just video quality

See also How Much Does It Cost To Run Webinars?

## Why Most Webinars Fail Before They Start

Ever registered for a webinar and received exactly zero reminder emails? Or joined an event only to watch the host struggle with screen sharing for ten awkward minutes while 200 people wait in silence? These failures don’t happen during the event—they happen during planning. Or rather, during the lack of planning.

Think about the last webinar you attended that actually impressed you. Chances are, you received a well-designed confirmation email immediately after registering. Then a reminder email three days before. Then another reminder one hour before. When you clicked the join link, you entered a branded waiting room with clear instructions and maybe even a poll to answer while waiting. The presentation started on time, the audio was crystal clear, and you received a recording within hours of the session ending.

None of that happens by accident. Every single touchpoint was planned, scheduled, and automated weeks before the event went live. The hosts didn’t just “wing it and hope for the best”—they built a system.

## The Hidden Complexity Behind Simple Webinars

From the outside, hosting a webinar looks straightforward: schedule a time, send some invitations, talk into your webcam for an hour. Simple, right? But peek behind the curtain of any successful webinar, and you’ll find dozens of interconnected decisions that all need answers:

How will you capture registrant data? What information do you actually need from attendees? When should reminder emails go out, and how many is too many? What happens if your main presenter’s internet connection fails? How will you transition between speakers? What happens to people who register after the event starts? Where will the recording be hosted? How do you measure success beyond just “attendance”?

See also How to Host a Webinar: A Step-by-Step Guide

These aren’t theoretical questions—they’re practical roadblocks that derail unprepared hosts every single day. The webinars that succeed treat planning as a discipline, not a chore.

## Expert’s Voice

> I’ve seen countless webinars with brilliant content fail spectacularly because the host skipped basic planning steps. You can have the world’s best presentation, but if attendees can’t figure out how to unmute themselves or your polls don’t work, nobody remembers your content—they remember the chaos. Planning isn’t glamorous, but it’s the difference between professional and amateur.

Tomasz Bolcun Brand Manager @ ClickMeeting

## Your Complete Webinar Planning Timeline

Let’s break down exactly what needs to happen, and when. This timeline assumes you’re planning a standard 60-minute live webinar, but you can adjust these timeframes based on your event’s complexity.

### 4-6 Weeks Before: Foundation and Strategy

This is when you make the big decisions that shape everything else. Start by defining your core objective with brutal clarity. Are you generating leads? Launching a product? Educating existing customers? Establishing thought leadership? Your objective determines literally everything else—from how you design registration forms to which metrics you’ll track afterward.

Action items for this phase:

- Define one primary goal and two secondary metrics
- Identify and confirm all speakers or panelists
- Choose your webinar platform based on planning features, not just video quality
- Create a detailed content outline with time allocations for each section
- Determine your ideal attendee profile and registration requirements
- Set up your event in your chosen platform and configure basic settings

Here’s something most planning guides won’t tell you: choose your webinar software based on how well it handles preparation and automation, not just streaming quality. Platforms like ClickMeeting offer integrated tools for everything from custom branded registration pages to automated email sequences, which means you’re building one cohesive system instead of duct-taping five different tools together.

### 3 Weeks Before: Content Development and Promotion Launch

Now you’re building the actual content while simultaneously starting to fill seats. These two tracks run parallel, and both demand attention.

Content development tasks:

- Finalize your presentation deck with speaker notes
- Create interactive elements (polls, Q&A segments, live demonstrations)
- Write scripts or talking points for transitions between sections
- Prepare backup content in case you finish early or need to fill time
- Design your custom waiting room with agenda and pre-event polls

Promotional tasks:

- Build your registration landing page with compelling copy
- Set up email automation sequences (confirmation, reminders, follow-ups)
- Create social media promotional graphics and posts
- Reach out to partners or affiliates for promotional support
- Set up tracking parameters to measure which promotional channels work best

When crafting your registration page, think like your audience. They’re asking themselves “What’s in this for me?” and “Can I trust these people with an hour of my time?” Your landing page needs to answer both questions immediately. Use specific outcomes (“Learn how to generate 300+ qualified leads per month”) instead of vague promises (“Improve your marketing”).

### 2 Weeks Before: Technical Setup and Dry Runs

This is where amateurs and professionals diverge dramatically. Professionals do complete technical rehearsals. Amateurs cross their fingers and hope technology cooperates.

Technical preparation essentials:

- Test all audio equipment and establish your backup audio solution
- Verify screen sharing works properly and all presenters know how to use it
- Practice transitions between speakers and content types
- Test interactive features (polls, Q&A, chat moderation) with your team
- Verify your internet connection speed and identify the strongest wifi spot
- Set up your presentation space with proper lighting and minimal background distractions

For any webinar expecting more than 50 attendees, schedule at least one full dress rehearsal with all speakers present. Run through the entire presentation as if it’s live, including all interactive elements and transitions. Time everything. Identify which segments run long and which feel rushed. Test what happens when you simulate technical problems—what if a presenter’s screen share fails? What if someone’s audio cuts out?

This sounds excessive until you experience your first technical meltdown during a live event with 500 people watching. Then it seems like the bare minimum.

### 1 Week Before: Final Touches and Promotion Push

You’re in the home stretch now. Most of your heavy lifting is complete, but this week separates good webinars from great ones.

Focus areas for the final week:

- Send your first reminder email to all registrants
- Post final promotional pushes across all channels with urgency messaging
- Prepare contingency plans for common scenarios (presenter no-show, platform issues, low attendance)
- Brief any moderators or co-hosts on their specific responsibilities
- Create your post-event follow-up email with recording link and next steps
- Schedule one final technical check 24 hours before going live
- Prepare engagement elements for the waiting room (polls, welcome message, music)

Many hosts make the mistake of going silent after someone registers, then sending one reminder the morning of the event. This is backwards. Your email sequence should nurture registrants throughout the waiting period, building anticipation and reinforcing the value they’ll receive. Consider sending an email one week out highlighting one key takeaway they’ll learn, then another three days before with social proof from previous events, then your final reminder on event day.

## The Technology Choice That Changes Everything

Let’s address the elephant in the room: platform selection. You’ve probably heard of the usual suspects—Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet. These work fine for internal meetings, but hosting a professional webinar requires different capabilities entirely.

What actually matters in webinar software:

First, scalability without complexity. Your registration list might say 200 people, but what if 500 show up? Some platforms require complicated enterprise contracts to handle large audiences, while others like ClickMeeting offer “Huge Virtual Events” mode that scales up to 10,000 viewers without requiring IT support or special configuration.

Second, automation that prevents human error. Manually tracking registrations in a spreadsheet and sending reminder emails from your Outlook? That’s a recipe for forgotten tasks and embarrassing mistakes. Modern webinar platforms automate the entire attendee journey—from confirmation emails when they register to automated follow-ups with recordings after the event ends.

Third, branding that builds authority. When your attendees join a webinar through a generic Zoom link and land in a basic waiting room with default settings, it screams “amateur hour.” Professional platforms allow custom branded registration pages, personalized waiting rooms with your logo and colors, and vanity URLs that reinforce your brand. First impressions matter, and they start before your presentation does.

Fourth, monetization capabilities if you’re running paid events. Setting up third-party payment processors and managing access tokens manually is a logistical nightmare. Integrated payment solutions handle everything—attendees purchase tickets, receive unique access links automatically, and you collect revenue through secure processors like Stripe or PayPal without touching a single spreadsheet.

Fifth, engagement tools that keep attendees active. Chat, polls, Q&A, whiteboard collaboration, breakout rooms—these aren’t nice-to-have extras anymore. They’re essential for maintaining attention in an environment where every attendee has Instagram, Slack, and Netflix just one browser tab away.

Platforms built specifically for webinars rather than general video calls understand these requirements. ClickMeeting, for instance, offers all these capabilities in one cohesive system designed around the planning process. You’re not trying to force a meeting tool to do webinar tasks—you’re using software purpose-built for events.

## Your Webinar Planning Checklist: From Concept to Completion

Here’s your comprehensive checklist organized by category. Use this as your master reference document for every webinar you plan.

### Strategic Planning

- Define one clear primary objective for this webinar
- Identify your target audience with specific demographic and psychographic details
- Determine success metrics (registration rate, attendance rate, engagement rate, conversion rate)
- Choose your webinar format (presentation, panel discussion, interview, Q&A, product demo)
- Select date and time based on audience timezone and behavior patterns
- Research competitor events to ensure you’re not scheduling during conflicts

### Content Development

- Create detailed content outline with time allocations for each segment
- Develop your main presentation with speaker notes
- Design custom slides optimized for screen sharing (high contrast, large text)
- Prepare interactive elements (polls with specific questions, Q&A segments)
- Write scripts for opening, transitions, and closing
- Create backup content for technical difficulties or early finish
- Develop post-event resources (slides, handouts, additional materials)

### Platform and Technical Setup

- Select webinar platform based on event requirements and attendee capacity
- Set up your event with correct date, time, and timezone settings
- Configure registration page with compelling copy and clear call-to-action
- Customize waiting room with branding, agenda, and pre-event polls
- Set up automated email sequences (confirmation, reminders, follow-ups)
- Test audio equipment and establish backup audio solution
- Verify internet connection speed and identify optimal broadcasting location
- Configure screen sharing and test with all presenters
- Set up engagement tools (chat moderation, poll creation, Q&A management)
- Create unique access links or passwords if needed for security

### Promotion and Registration

- Build registration landing page with social proof and value proposition
- Set up email marketing campaigns across your subscriber list
- Create social media promotional graphics and schedule posts
- Reach out to partners and affiliates for promotional support
- Set up tracking parameters to measure promotional effectiveness
- Consider paid advertising if budget allows (LinkedIn, Facebook, Google)
- Add event to relevant calendars and event listing sites

### Team Coordination

- Confirm all speakers and brief them on format and expectations
- Assign roles (presenter, moderator, technical support, chat monitor)
- Schedule and conduct full dress rehearsal with all team members
- Create run-of-show document with minute-by-minute breakdown
- Establish communication method for team during live event (Slack, text)
- Prepare contingency plans for common issues (presenter no-show, technical failure)

### Day-Of Preparation

- Join platform 30 minutes early to test all systems
- Verify audio, video, and screen sharing functionality
- Load presentation and test transitions
- Welcome early arrivals and engage in waiting room chat
- Brief team on any last-minute changes
- Have backup contact information for all speakers readily available
- Keep water nearby and silence all notifications

### Post-Event Follow-Up

- Send automated thank-you email with recording link
- Upload recording to hosting platform and ensure accessibility
- Send survey to gather attendee feedback
- Analyze performance metrics against initial goals
- Download attendee list and engagement data for CRM
- Follow up with high-engagement attendees for conversion opportunities
- Document lessons learned for next event improvement
- Share highlights and key quotes on social media

## The Art of Webinar Engagement Planning

Here’s something most planning guides ignore: engagement doesn’t happen spontaneously during your webinar. It’s planned, structured, and deliberately built into your event design from the beginning.

Think about traditional in-person conferences. Nobody just stands at a podium talking for three hours straight. There are breaks, networking sessions, interactive workshops, Q&A panels. Your webinar needs the same intentional variety, but compressed into a shorter timeframe.

Engagement strategy for different webinar lengths:

For a 30-minute webinar, plan two interaction points—one poll at the 10-minute mark and a Q&A segment for the final five minutes. For a 60-minute webinar, increase to four interaction points—opening poll, mid-presentation audience question, demonstration where attendees can participate, and final Q&A. For 90+ minute webinars, add breakout room discussions or interactive workshops where smaller groups collaborate.

The psychology here matters more than the technology. When you ask attendees to actively participate—even something as simple as answering a poll—you’re triggering the commitment bias. They’ve invested effort into your event, which makes them more likely to stay engaged and less likely to tab over to email or Instagram.

Your waiting room represents your first engagement opportunity that most hosts completely waste. Instead of silence or generic hold music, use this time productively. Display your agenda so latecomers know exactly what they missed. Launch a poll asking attendees where they’re joining from or what their biggest challenge is. Start a chat discussion with a provocative question related to your topic. Make people feel like they’re part of something happening now, not just passive observers of a recorded presentation.

## Common Planning Mistakes That Tank Attendance

You’ve done everything right—created compelling content, built a beautiful landing page, promoted across multiple channels. Then webinar day arrives and only 40% of registrants actually show up. What happened?

The reminder email gap: Most no-shows happen because people genuinely forgot. They registered three weeks ago with good intentions, then life happened. Send at least three reminder emails—one week before, one day before, and one hour before. Each reminder should include the join link prominently and reinforce one specific value point they’ll learn.

The timezone confusion: You’re based in New York and automatically list times in Eastern. Half your audience is in California trying to do timezone math in their heads, getting confused, and missing the start. Modern webinar platforms automatically display times in each registrant’s local timezone. Use this feature. If your platform doesn’t offer it, explicitly list multiple timezones in all communications.

The calendar invite omission: People manage their schedules through calendar apps, not email folders. When someone registers, automatically generate a calendar invite they can add with one click. This puts your event in the same place they track every other commitment, dramatically improving attendance rates.

The generic registration page: Your landing page looks like every other webinar registration form—bland, corporate, full of jargon. People skim it, think “maybe later,” and close the tab. Your registration page needs to answer three questions in the first 10 seconds: What will I learn? Why should I trust you? What happens after I register? Use specific outcomes, social proof, and clear next steps.

The missing value proposition: Your promotional materials talk about what you’ll cover, not what attendees will gain. “Learn about email marketing strategies” is boring. “Discover the exact email sequence that generated 760,000 PLN in revenue for one accounting firm” is compelling. Specificity sells.

## Advanced Planning: Preparing for Problems

Murphy’s Law applies doubly to live webinars. Whatever can go wrong eventually will. Professional webinar hosts don’t prevent all problems—they prepare contingencies so problems don’t derail the event.

Critical backup systems to implement:

Audio failure is the number one technical disaster. Your primary microphone stops working or your internet connection cuts out. Your backup? A phone dial-in number that lets you join your own webinar by audio. Many platforms including ClickMeeting offer dial-in options. Keep the number saved on your phone before the event starts.

Presentation file corruption happens more than you’d think. Your carefully crafted PowerPoint decides to corrupt itself 10 minutes before going live. Your backup? Upload your presentation to your webinar platform the day before. Even if your local file fails, the cloud-hosted version is ready.

Presenter no-shows create awkward dead air unless you’ve prepared filler content. Your guest expert gets stuck in traffic or double-booked themselves. Your backup? Have supplementary content ready—additional case studies, extra Q&A time, or pre-recorded segments you can show. Always prepare 20% more content than you think you’ll need.

Internet instability causes freezing, dropping, and frustrated attendees. Your home wifi starts struggling under load. Your backup? Identify the strongest wifi location in your space beforehand. Consider using an ethernet connection instead of wireless. Have mobile hotspot capability from your phone as an emergency internet source.

Platform failure is rare but catastrophic when it happens. Your chosen webinar platform experiences unexpected downtime. Your backup? This is why you should know how to quickly set up a backup stream on an alternative platform. Keep Zoom or Google Meet credentials ready just in case.

## Measuring Success: Beyond Attendance Numbers

You hosted your webinar. The attendance rate was solid at 55%. Your content was well-received. Now what? How do you know if the event was actually successful?

Attendance rate tells you people showed up, but not whether they stayed or engaged. Look at average watch time—did attendees stay for 15 minutes or the full 60? Check engagement metrics like poll responses, chat messages, and Q&A questions submitted. ClickMeeting’s analytics dashboard breaks down these metrics so you can identify which segments held attention and which lost viewers.

Conversion rate matters more than attendance for most business objectives. If your goal was lead generation, how many attendees downloaded your resource, requested a demo, or scheduled a consultation? Track this through unique links or UTM parameters in your follow-up emails. A webinar with 100 attendees that generates 30 qualified leads outperforms one with 500 attendees that generates 10.

Post-event engagement reveals true interest levels. Who watched the recording? Who forwarded the replay to colleagues? Who responded to your follow-up survey? These behaviors indicate genuine interest versus passive attendance. Set up tracking for recording views and engagement with post-event materials.

Revenue attribution shows direct financial impact. For paid webinars, this is straightforward—ticket sales minus costs equals profit. For lead generation webinars, track which attendees eventually become customers and calculate customer lifetime value. This data justifies your webinar program’s existence when leadership asks about ROI.

Qualitative feedback provides insights numbers can’t capture. Send a brief survey asking what attendees found most valuable and what could improve. Read through chat logs to identify questions you didn’t address. Review social media mentions to see how people are talking about your event. This intelligence directly improves your next webinar.

## FAQ Section

How far in advance should I start planning a webinar? Start planning 4-6 weeks before your target date for standard webinars. This gives you adequate time for content development, speaker coordination, promotional campaigns, and technical rehearsals. High-stakes webinars with multiple speakers or complex topics may require 8-12 weeks of lead time.

What’s the ideal webinar length? Most effective webinars run 45-60 minutes including Q&A. Shorter than 30 minutes feels too brief to deliver substantial value, while longer than 75 minutes causes attention fatigue. If your content requires more time, consider a multi-session series instead of one marathon event.

How many reminder emails should I send without annoying registrants? Three reminders represent the sweet spot: one week before, one day before, and one hour before the event. Each serves a different purpose—the week-out reminder builds anticipation, the day-before reminder ensures calendar blocking, and the hour-before reminder catches people who forgot despite good intentions.

What’s a good registration-to-attendance conversion rate? Industry averages hover around 40-50%, meaning if 100 people register, expect 40-50 to actually attend. Rates above 60% indicate excellent promotional messaging and reminder sequences. Rates below 30% suggest problems with your registration quality or follow-up communication.

Should I require registration for free webinars? Yes, always require registration even for free events. Registration gives you contact information for follow-up, helps you estimate attendance for capacity planning, reduces no-show rates (people who register feel more committed), and provides data for understanding your audience demographics.

What information should I collect during registration? At minimum, collect name and email address. For B2B webinars, add company name, job title, and company size to qualify leads. Balance information gathering with conversion optimization—each additional field reduces registration rates by approximately 5-10%. Only ask for data you’ll actually use.

How do I choose between live and automated webinars? Use live webinars when real-time interaction adds significant value—product launches, time-sensitive topics, or events where Q&A is critical. Use automated webinars when you’re delivering consistent educational content repeatedly, need to accommodate multiple timezones, or want to scale without additional presenter time. Many hosts create live webinars initially, then convert high-performing events to automated replays.

What’s the best day and time to host a webinar? Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday mornings (10-11 AM) or early afternoons (1-2 PM) in your audience’s timezone typically perform best for B2B audiences. Avoid Monday mornings (too busy) and Friday afternoons (mentally checked out). For consumer audiences, evening times (6-8 PM) often work better when people are home from work.

How much should I budget for webinar software? Professional webinar platforms range from $40-$200+ per month depending on attendee capacity, features, and hosting frequency. Calculate cost-per-attendee by dividing monthly subscription by expected monthly attendees. Platforms offering automation, branding, and integrated analytics typically provide better ROI than basic video conferencing tools despite higher upfront costs.

What happens if technical issues occur during my live webinar? Stay calm and have backup plans ready. If audio fails, use your phone dial-in option. If screen sharing breaks, describe content verbally while troubleshooting. If your platform crashes entirely, immediately email all registrants with a backup meeting link. Most importantly, communicate transparently with attendees rather than going silent while you panic-troubleshoot behind the scenes.

Riverside Webinar Tutorial (2026): Setup & Host | Feisworld Media

After I published my comparison of the best webinar platforms in 2026, the number one question I got was: “Can you actually walk me through how to set up a Riverside webinar step by step?” Fair enough. Knowing that Riverside records in 4K and has Magic Clips is one thing. Actually setting up a webinar from scratch: building your registration page, configuring reminder emails, going live, and turning the recording into content afterward. That is a different conversation entirely. So I did it.

I recorded the entire process on video, and this article is the written companion. Think of it as the guide you can keep open in a tab while you build your first Riverside webinar. If you have never used Riverside before, or if you have only used it for podcast recording and want to explore the webinar side, this walkthrough is for you.

## Watch the Full Riverside Webinar Tutorial

If you prefer to see every click and setting in action, here is the companion video. The article below follows the same walkthrough step by step.

---

## TL;DR: What You Will Learn in This Riverside Webinar Walkthrough

If you are short on time, here is what this Riverside webinar tutorial covers:

- Scheduling a webinar from your Riverside dashboard (takes about 2 minutes)
- Building a registration page with custom fields, branding, and CRM integration
- Setting up automated reminder emails so attendees actually show up
- Going live — what the studio looks like, layouts, screen sharing, and the teleprompter
- Livestreaming to social media (YouTube, LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitch, X, TikTok, custom RTMP)
- Recording settings — choosing between 720p, 1080p, and 4K
- Audience engagement — public chat, Q&A, polls, and studio chat for your production team
- Post-webinar repurposing — accessing your recording, downloading tracks, and using Magic Clips and Magic Segments

If you want a deeper look at how Magic Clips work for content repurposing, I wrote a full step-by-step guide to creating YouTube Shorts with Riverside earlier this year.

---

## Why I Moved My Webinars to Riverside

I have hosted hundreds of webinars. For years, the default was Zoom Webinar. It worked, it scaled, and everyone knew how to join.

But here is what kept happening: after the webinar ended, I would download the recording and get a blurry, compressed file that looked like it was filmed through a window screen.

That is not just a branding problem. That is a content problem. If you are spending two weeks preparing a webinar and the recording is unwatchable on YouTube, you just lost your entire repurposing pipeline.

Riverside’s webinar software solves this because it records locally on each participant’s device. Your internet connection affects the live stream quality, but the actual recording — the file you keep and repurpose — is captured at up to 4K resolution directly on your computer.

That distinction changes everything for creators and marketers who treat webinars as content production sessions, not just live events.

Riverside now has a dedicated webinar product with registration pages, automated emails, live chat, Q&A, polls, call-ins, multistreaming, and post-event analytics. The self-serve Webinar tier includes HubSpot; Salesforce and Marketo are listed on Business. That distinction matters if CRM depth or a production team is part of your buying decision.

It is no longer a recording tool that people hack into a webinar setup. It is a complete webinar platform.

## Step 1: Schedule Your Webinar

From your Riverside homepage, click the Schedule button. On the right side, click New and then select Webinar.

Here is what you will fill in:

- Webinar name: Give it a clear title—this appears on the registration page.
- Date and time: Schedule ahead or create a near-term session; confirm the displayed time zone before sharing the link.
- Invite speakers: Guests are the on-camera presenters. If you need a dedicated behind-the-scenes producer with advanced input controls, confirm Business-plan access rather than assuming it is part of the self-serve Webinar tier.
- Description: Add a concise summary of the promise and who the webinar is for. You can invite speakers later from the session.

### Advanced Option: Pre-Recorded Content

Before you move on, there is one feature worth knowing about. Under Advanced, you can upload pre-recorded video (MP4) or audio (MP3, WAV) to play during your webinar. This is useful for product demo segments, intro videos, or polished presentations where you want produced footage instead of live delivery.

## Step 2: Build Your Registration Page

This is where Riverside’s webinar setup surprised me the most. The registration system is fully built in — no need for a separate landing page tool, Eventbrite, or Zapier automation.

### Registration Form

You can customize the form fields to collect exactly what you need:

Title and description — what the event is about and who is hosting it.

Custom fields — by default it asks for name and email. But you can add phone number, country, and even custom text fields, single-selection dropdowns, and checkboxes. This matters if you are qualifying leads before the event starts.

My recommendation: keep the form short. Every additional field creates friction. For a marketing webinar, name and email is usually enough. If you need lead qualification data (job title, company size), add one or two custom fields maximum.

### Visual Branding

You can upload a background image and your company logo directly onto the registration page. There is also an option to hide the Riverside logo for a fully white-labeled look. The result is a clean, branded registration page you can share via email, social media, or embed on your website.

### CRM Integration: HubSpot on Webinar; Salesforce on Business

On the Webinar plan, Riverside lists HubSpot lead sync. Salesforce and Marketo are Business features. Registrant exports remain useful when your CRM is not connected, but confirm which attendance and source fields are available in your workspace before promising them to a sales team.

This is a major upgrade for anyone using webinars as part of a demand generation strategy.

## Step 3: Set Up Reminder Emails

This is small but critical. In my own webinar work, the one-day and one-hour reminders are the messages I would not skip. They reduce the chance that an interested registrant simply loses the event in a crowded calendar.

Riverside gives you three built-in options:

1. One day before the event — catches people who registered early and might forget.
2. One hour before the event — this is the most impactful reminder. It catches busy people right before showtime.
3. Post-event follow-up — sends automatically after the webinar ends. Perfect for sharing the replay link, a summary, or a CTA.

I recommend turning on all three. If you have run webinars before, you know how much attendance improves when people get that one-hour nudge.

## My Five-Minute Riverside Webinar Preflight

After hosting hundreds of webinars, this is the check I run before an attendee arrives:

1. Open the studio in the browser and device you will actually use. Approve camera, microphone, and screen-recording permissions before showtime.
2. Record 30 seconds. Play it back through headphones and listen for echo, clipping, fan noise, or the wrong microphone.
3. Verify every role and link. A speaker link, audience watch link, and producer workflow are not interchangeable.
4. Load the slides, pre-recorded media, poll, and live CTA. Put them in run-of-show order so the host is not searching while live.
5. Write down the fallback. Keep a co-host contact channel, the direct watch link, and a local copy of the presentation within reach.

This preflight is less exciting than a new AI feature, but it has saved more live events for me than any single tool.

## Step 4: Start Your Webinar Session, Inside the Riverside Studio

When it is time to go live, click Start Session from your webinar dashboard. This does not immediately broadcast to your audience — you land in a pre-session setup screen where you can verify your camera, microphone, audio output, and display name.

Once you click Join Studio, you are inside the webinar environment. Even at this point, attendees cannot see you. You are in a private backstage view.

The live broadcast begins only when you click the red Record button. At that moment, two things happen simultaneously: your webinar starts recording locally in high quality, and it goes live to registered attendees.

## Step 5: Layouts and Screen Sharing

Riverside offers several layout options you can switch between during the live session:

- Full Screen: Just you (or your shared content), no split.
- Grid Fill: Equal split between all speakers — ideal for panel discussions.
- Split Screen: One speaker takes roughly two-thirds of the frame, the other one-third. Good for interviews where you want to highlight the guest.
- Landscape View: Side-by-side speakers.
- Picture-in-Picture (Circle): Your face appears in a small circle overlaid on your shared content. My go-to for slide presentations — you stay visible without covering key information.
- Picture-in-Picture (Square): Same concept, slightly larger and rectangular.

These layouts matter more than people think. If you are presenting slides, picture-in-picture keeps your face visible so the audience stays connected. If you are running a panel, grid fill gives everyone equal screen presence.

### Screen Sharing

Click Share to share your screen or a specific window. One important note: if this is your first time, Chrome will ask for screen recording permission. Test this before your live session — you do not want to troubleshoot browser permissions in front of your audience. Once sharing is active, the layout options update to show how your shared content and camera feed are arranged together.

## Step 6: Use the Teleprompter

This is one of my favorite Riverside features that most webinar hosts do not know about. Inside the studio, click Script in the bottom toolbar.

You can type your talking points, key phrases, or a full script directly into Riverside. When you are ready, click Teleprompter to switch to a scrolling view centered on your screen.

Here is why this matters: if you position the teleprompter window near your webcam, you can read your notes while maintaining natural eye contact with the camera. No more glancing down at Post-it notes or a second monitor.

You can adjust the scroll speed, pause and restart at any time, and resize the teleprompter window. I recommend practicing with it for a few minutes before going live to find your comfortable reading pace.

## Step 7: Livestream to Social Media

You do not have to multistream — you can simply run the webinar for registered attendees and record it.

Riverside currently lists direct multistreaming to YouTube, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, and Twitch, plus custom RTMP for other destinations. Connection options change, so verify the destination in your own dashboard before advertising a simulcast.

You can configure these before or during the session. Each platform requires a one-time connection to your account.

Pro tip: Even if you do not multistream to social media, Riverside generates a Watch Link — a simple URL where anyone can view your webinar live. If you enabled registration, viewers will be prompted to register first. This gives you flexibility: share the link publicly and still capture lead data.

### Livestream vs. Recording Quality — The Key Distinction

This is important to understand. The live stream broadcasts at up to 1080p, depending on your internet connection. But the recording — the file saved locally on your device — captures at whatever resolution you choose: 720p, 1080p, or 4K.

Because each participant's high-quality track is recorded locally and uploaded progressively, a brief network problem does not automatically ruin the recorded file. A device, browser, or extended connection failure can still interrupt a track, which is why I record the preflight sample and keep a fallback plan.

## Step 8: Engage Your Audience — Chat, Q&A, and Polls

The right side of the Riverside webinar studio has two communication channels:

### Public Chat

This is visible to everyone watching. Attendees can send messages, ask questions, and react in real time. Within the public chat, you also have access to: Q&A: A dedicated section where audience questions appear separately from general chat.

This makes it easy to track, prioritize, and respond to questions without losing them in the chat scroll. Polls: You can create polls and survey your audience during the session. Great for boosting engagement, gathering feedback, or making interactive decisions live.

### Studio Chat (Private)

This is visible only to presenters and producers. Use it for behind-the-scenes coordination — timing cues, technical notes, or deciding which audience question to address next. No more texting your producer on WhatsApp during a live session.

### Live Call-Ins

Audience members can request to be brought on-screen during the webinar. If you approve the request, they join the live session temporarily — like a call-in segment on a talk show. They are recorded for the duration of the call-in but do not count toward your 10-speaker limit.

## Step 9: Additional Studio Features

A few more features inside the Riverside webinar studio that are worth knowing about:

### Branding on the Fly

Under the Branding tab, you can adjust your logo, background, and design elements even while live. There are also overlay options for lower thirds and visual elements.

### Live Links

You can create clickable links that appear on screen during the webinar. Type the URL and display text, save it, and show or hide as needed. When attendees click, it takes them directly to that destination. Excellent for promoting a product page, a special offer, or a resource download during your session.

### Media Uploads

In the interface I tested, I could upload MP4 or MOV media for intros, demos, and testimonials. Upload limits and supported formats can change, so load and preview every asset before the live session instead of discovering a limit on air.

### Preview vs. Live Mode

There is a toggle between Preview and Live. Preview means only you see and hear whatever you are testing. Live means it goes out to your audience. Always test new content, layouts, or media in Preview mode first — it is your safety net.

## Step 10: Recording Settings

Before or during your session, click the gear icon to configure your recording:

- 720p: Fastest upload and processing after the webinar. Good enough if you just need a quick replay.
- 1080p: My usual choice. Strong balance of quality and processing speed for most content needs.
- 4K (UHD): Maximum quality. Conversion takes longer, but the output is broadcast-grade. Choose this if the webinar recording will become a YouTube video or flagship marketing content.

You can also configure:

- Transcript language: Dozens of languages are supported, including Chinese — which, as a bilingual creator, I genuinely appreciate.
- Noise reduction: If you or your speakers are in noisy environments, enable this to clean up the recording automatically.

## After the Webinar: Recordings and AI-Powered Repurposing

This is where Riverside’s webinar product earns its keep. Once the session ends, go to Projects in your dashboard to find the recording.

### What You Get

- Combined recording: All participants merged into one video file.
- Individual tracks: Separate audio and video files for each speaker. Invaluable for editing — you can adjust each person’s audio independently or cut between camera angles in your video editor.
- Aligned video: If guests joined at different times, this feature syncs all timelines automatically so your editor can line everything up instantly.
- Raw vs. compressed audio: Choose which format to download based on your workflow.

### AI Content Repurposing: Magic Clips, Segments, and More

Under the Made for You tab, Riverside uses AI to generate content from your webinar recording automatically:

Magic Episode: An AI-polished edit of the full recording with cleaned-up audio and auto-generated show notes.

Magic Clips: Short vertical clips (usually under 60 seconds) pulled from your best moments. They come with captions and are ready for Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, TikTok, and LinkedIn. Each clip gets a Viral Score so you know which ones are most likely to perform well. (I wrote a full guide to Magic Clips and Viral Scores here.)

Magic Segments: Longer landscape clips (2–5 minutes) that work beautifully for YouTube and LinkedIn. These are my personal favorites because they give a guest enough time to finish a complete thought — which builds more authority than a 15-second sound bite.

Hooks: Short attention-grabbing openings designed to pull viewers in.

Posts: AI-generated social media copy based on the webinar content.

Snapshots: Key visual moments captured as still images. From a single one-hour webinar, you can walk away with a dozen or more content assets without ever opening an editing timeline.

### Registrant Data and Lead Tracking

Your registrant table includes names, emails, custom field responses, registration source, and total minutes attended. You can download this as a CSV or sync it directly to HubSpot as contact properties. This data is the bridge between your webinar as a content event and your webinar as a lead generation engine. You know exactly who showed up, how long they stayed, and how they found you.

## How This Fits Into a 2026 Webinar Content Strategy

Let me be direct about why this matters.

In 2026, the creators, consultants, and marketing teams who win are the ones who extract the most value from every piece of content they produce. A webinar is not a one-time live event anymore. It is a content production session.

Here is the workflow I recommend:

1. Host the webinar on Riverside — capture leads through registration, engage the audience live, and record everything in high quality.
2. Repurpose immediately — use Magic Clips and Magic Segments to generate social content the same day the webinar airs.
3. Publish the full recording on YouTube — the 4K recording quality means it stands on its own as a long-form video.
4. Write a companion blog post — embed the video, add SEO-optimized text, and create an evergreen page that drives organic traffic long after the live event.
5. Feed registrant data into your CRM — follow up with leads, segment by engagement level, and nurture toward your offer.

One webinar. Five content channels. That is the shift from “hosting events” to building a content engine.

Sources checked July 18, 2026: Riverside plans and pricing and the Riverside webinar help center.

## Riverside Webinar Pricing (2026)

Riverside currently lists Webinar at $99/month on monthly billing or $79/month billed annually. That tier includes three studios, 25 hours of separate-track downloads, up to 100 registrants, branded registration, reminders, Q&A, polls, analytics, pre-recorded webinars, embeds, and HubSpot integration. Capacity above 100 and Salesforce/Marketo require Business.

For context, Riverside lists Pro at $29 monthly/$24 annually and Grow at $39 monthly/$34 annually. Grow adds live streaming, but Riverside says you need at least Webinar for registration, Q&A, polls, reminder emails, and webinar analytics.

Riverside also offers a free plan with limited recording time and basic features, so you can test the interface and editing tools before committing.

All paid plans include a 14-day free trial. Use code FEI to get one month free on Riverside Pro or Livestream plans, plus a discount when you upgrade to the Webinar plan.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Can I run a webinar on Riverside’s free plan?

Riverside’s free plan includes basic recording capabilities, but the full webinar features — registration pages, automated reminder emails, audience management, CRM sync — require the Webinar plan starting at $79/month. You can use the free plan to test Riverside’s recording and editing tools before upgrading.

How many people can attend a Riverside webinar?

The self-serve Webinar plan supports up to 100 registrants. Riverside lists up to 10,000 webinar registrants on Business. Multistreaming can extend public reach, but it does not turn the self-serve registration cap into an unlimited audience.

How many speakers can be on screen?

Riverside lists up to 10 people recorded in one session. Advanced producer mode and production roles are Business features, so confirm the role controls you need before planning a complex panel.

Do attendees need to download anything?

No. Riverside webinars run entirely in the browser. Attendees click a link and watch — no app download required. This removes one of the biggest friction points that platforms like Zoom still have.

Can I integrate Riverside webinars with my CRM?

Riverside lists HubSpot on the self-serve Webinar plan; Salesforce and Marketo are on Business. You can also export registrant data, which is the practical fallback when your CRM is not natively connected.

What happens if my internet drops during the webinar?

The live stream may be affected. Riverside's local, progressive recording is designed to preserve higher-quality participant tracks through brief network instability, but no platform can protect a recording from every device, browser, power, or extended connection failure. Record a sample and keep a backup.

Can I use the teleprompter during a live webinar?

Yes. Riverside’s built-in teleprompter lets you load a script, adjust scroll speed, and position the window near your webcam for natural eye contact. It works during webinars exactly like it does in standard recording sessions.

Is Riverside webinar software better than Zoom Webinar?

It depends on your priorities. I prefer Riverside when the webinar recording will become YouTube, podcast, or social content because local separate tracks and built-in repurposing are central to the workflow. Zoom may fit better when your organization prioritizes established meeting administration, larger event packages, or specific enterprise controls. My webinar platform comparison explains the trade-off in more detail.

## Feisworld’s Take: Your Webinar Should Be a Production Session

If you are still running webinars on Zoom and downloading grainy recordings that sit in a folder, I want you to try one Riverside webinar. Just one.

Set up the registration page. Invite a guest. Go live.

And then look at what you have when it is over: the option for a high-resolution local recording, separate participant tracks, repurposing drafts, and registrant data you can act on. The exact output depends on your plan, settings, and source quality; this is a production workflow, not a guarantee that every AI clip is publish-ready.

That is not just a webinar. That is a content production session. And in 2026, that is exactly what a webinar should be.

## Summary
In 2026, practitioner walkthroughs for WebinarJam, Zoom, and Riverside show that successful webinars hinge on tight platform setup, deliberate interactivity (directed chat prompts, timed polls, planted open loops, and well-timed calls-to-action), and post-event repurposing workflows. Below are teardown-style runbooks that map those mechanics onto the concrete, step-by-step tutorials and capabilities documented in the 2026 sources, plus clear notes on what the sources do not substantiate [1][3][4][6][7][8].

## Key Findings
1) The core levers of engagement are directed chat prompts, strategically timed polls, planted open loops, and timed CTA overlays; these mechanics affect stick rate and conversion, and can be implemented even in automated formats [4].

2) Zoom’s 2026 materials and tutorials cover end-to-end webinar execution: scheduling, inviting participants, enabling polls, and managing Q&A, with both beginner and advanced walkthroughs available [7][8][3].

3) WebinarJam’s 2026 “Complete Setup Guide” (the written companion to Austin Marland’s 29‑minute walkthrough) walks through every screen and setting decision to take you from a blank account to a live broadcast in one sitting [1].

4) Riverside’s 2026 tutorial shows how to set up and host a webinar; Riverside records in 4K and includes Magic Clips, which directly supports efficient content repurposing from the recording [6].

5) Minimal-setup workflows for professional webinars are available, including a 13:55 “Easiest Way to Host a Live Webinar in 2026” tutorial (published 2026‑03‑19) that demonstrates a low‑complexity path to going live [2].

6) 2026 planning guides emphasize upfront coordination and promotion; ClickMeeting’s guide (updated November 28, 2025) frames planning as a checklist-driven process involving speaker coordination and crafting promotion, aligning with the need to prepare registration and communication assets before going live [5].

7) The sources here do not substantiate specific “ideal length,” “best send cadence for reminders,” or “industry-average drop‑off curve” numbers. Treat widely repeated figures on these topics as unverified within this corpus [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

## Detail

Session structure and running order (with platform mapping)
- Opening and orientation
  - Use a directed chat prompt as the very first audience touch to prime interaction (e.g., “Where are you joining from?” or “What’s your role?”), aligning with the “directed chat prompts” mechanic [4].
  - On Zoom, enable and monitor Chat and Q&A so responses have a visible home; Zoom tutorials explicitly show managing Q&A and enabling polls (you’ll set these up before the session) [7]. Zoom’s advanced tips guidance indicates there are additional configuration options to polish delivery [8]. Zoom’s own events resource frames these as best practices for a professional experience [3].
  - On WebinarJam, the 2026 setup guide takes you “through every screen and every setting decision,” so your opening flow can be configured end-to-end before you go live (the tutorial’s scope covers the live broadcast setup in full) [1].
  - On Riverside, follow the 2026 tutorial to set up your studio and guest flow; the platform’s 4K recording means your live environment is also optimized for later reuse [6].

- Core content with embedded engagement
  - Planted open loops: tease a later reveal or resource early (“I’ll show the template we used near the end”), then close the loop during the offer moment. This is one of the four named mechanics and is specifically positioned to maintain stick rate [4].
  - Strategically timed polls: schedule polls to punctuate content blocks and diagnose audience needs in-session. On Zoom, enabling polls and running them live is part of the 2026 hosting tutorial [7]. EasyWebinar’s guidance emphasizes timing as the lever (not merely having a poll), so place them before transitions or after a key point to regain attention [4].
  - Q&A interludes: Zoom supports managed Q&A sessions; make these short interludes to reset attention and surface objections early [7]. WebinarJam and Riverside setup tutorials are end-to-end, so plan similar interludes within those platforms’ interaction tools as configured during setup [1][6].

- Offer and conversion moment
  - Timed CTA overlays at the offer moment are one of the four mechanics. If your platform supports a visible, timed CTA element, schedule it to coincide with closing your biggest open loop [4]. (Note: the availability and exact implementation of CTA overlays vary by platform; the sources here document the principle and do not enumerate overlay support across Zoom/WebinarJam/Riverside [4][1][7][6].)

- Close and next steps
  - Summarize decisions and outcomes; if using Zoom, leave Q&A open briefly, which is covered as a managed element in the 2026 tutorial [7].
  - Recordings: Riverside’s 4K capture and Magic Clips directly support turning the session into short-form assets afterward [6]. If you hosted elsewhere, export the recording (platform-specific export steps are not detailed in these sources) and apply the same repurposing logic.

How to open strong
- Start with a directed chat prompt to create immediate audience action (this is explicitly called out as a core mechanic) [4].
- State one open loop early and reference its payoff time (“I’ll reveal the checklist later”), which EasyWebinar frames as a stick-rate lever [4].
- If polls are available (Zoom tutorial shows enabling them), run a quick early poll to segment or surface expectations [7][4].

Keeping attention across the full session
- Use the four mechanics as your backbone: direct chat prompts, timed polls, planted open loops, and timed CTAs [4].
- On Zoom, combine these with managed Q&A to break up monologues (capability shown in the 2026 Zoom guide) [7]. The advanced tips video indicates additional configuration and polish, which can reduce friction and maintain engagement quality [8].
- For automated/evergreen sessions, EasyWebinar notes interactivity can still be implemented (e.g., scheduled interactions), preserving stick-rate levers even when not live [4].

Interaction and polling technique (with platform examples)
- Technique: Don’t ask for “any questions?”; use directed prompts that produce a specific, scannable stream in chat, then escalate into a poll at key beats [4].
- Zoom example: Pre-create polls and enable them (as shown in the 2026 step-by-step tutorial), then trigger at transitions (“Before we switch topics, answer this…”) [7][4].
- Cross-platform principle: Plant open loops early, time the CTA to coincide with closing those loops, and use interaction points as attention resets rather than add-ons [4].

Length choices
- The sources here do not provide validated benchmarks or recommended durations. If you encounter widely repeated claims (e.g., ideal length targets), they are not traceable to the provided materials and should be treated as unverified within this set [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

Registration and reminder sequences
- Zoom’s 2026 tutorial shows scheduling webinars and inviting participants, which covers the platform-side mechanics of getting people registered and in the room [7]. Zoom’s official events guide positions these within broader best practices for hosting and managing virtual experiences [3].
- ClickMeeting’s 2026 planning guide emphasizes a checklist-driven approach to planning and promotion, indicating you should coordinate speakers and craft promotional assets in advance [5].
- None of the sources here specify reminder cadences or message counts; any repeated “X emails at Y hours” formulas are not substantiated in this corpus [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

Handling drop-off partway through
- EasyWebinar ties stick rate to interactivity and specifically prescribes planted open loops and strategically timed polls to hold attention through the midpoint [4].
- Insert an interaction just before and after your expected transition points; on Zoom, that means scheduling and launching polls and then collecting Q&A (capabilities covered in the 2026 tutorial) [7]. While many industry claims exist about when drop-off occurs, the provided sources do not publish those curves [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

Repurposing the recording
- Riverside: Record in 4K and use Magic Clips to create short, shareable segments efficiently; the 2026 tutorial is explicitly positioned to take you through setup and hosting, and cites Magic Clips as a post-production aid [6].
- If you hosted on Zoom or WebinarJam, export the recording (export steps not covered in these sources) and apply the same clip-first approach; the principle is to plan open loops and segment breaks in your run-of-show so they naturally become standalone clips post-event [4][6].

Worked examples and practitioner walkthroughs (annotated)

A) Zoom run-of-show (2026), assembled from Zoom’s how‑to plus EasyWebinar’s engagement mechanics
- Before the event: 
  - Schedule the webinar, invite participants, and enable polls per the 2026 Zoom tutorial [7]. 
  - Prepare directed chat prompts, poll questions, and at least one open loop to plant early [4].
- Live opening:
  - Launch a directed chat prompt immediately [4]; verify Q&A is active [7].
- Mid-session:
  - Trigger a strategically timed poll at a topic transition [7][4].
  - Insert a short Q&A interlude to surface objections [7].
  - Plant or reference open loops to sustain stick rate [4].
- Offer:
  - Present your CTA and, if your platform supports it, time a visible overlay to coincide with closing the biggest open loop [4].
- Close:
  - Final Q&A (managed via Zoom’s Q&A) [7].

B) WebinarJam (2026) teardown anchored to platform setup flow
- Use Austin Marland’s 29‑minute walkthrough companion guide to go “from a blank account to a live broadcast,” following “every screen and every setting decision” to configure your full session in one sitting [1].
- Layer in EasyWebinar’s interaction mechanics: draft directed chat prompts, schedule poll moments, and script open loops that you’ll close at the offer [4].
- Go live following the configured flow; the guide’s step-by-step nature reduces mid-session guesswork [1].

C) Riverside (2026) webinar with built-in repurposing
- Set up and host using the Riverside step-by-step tutorial [6].
- During the session, execute directed chat prompts and timed polls (if you’re layering in interactions via your chosen webinar flow) and plant open loops [4].
- After the event, leverage Riverside’s 4K recording quality and Magic Clips to create short-form assets from key beats you planned (poll results reveal, loop closure, top answer from Q&A) [6][4].

D) “Easiest way” minimal workflow
- If you need the quickest path, consult the 13:55 “Easiest Way to Host a Live Webinar in 2026” tutorial (published 2026‑03‑19) for a low‑complexity setup that still yields professional results [2]. Then apply the four engagement mechanics on top [4].

Current platform specifications and dates (as evidenced in sources)
- WebinarJam: 2026 complete setup guide covering every screen/setting; companion to Austin Marland’s 29‑minute walkthrough [1].
- Zoom: 2026 tutorials explicitly show scheduling, inviting, enabling polls, and managing Q&A; an advanced 2026 tips video is also available; Zoom’s resource center outlines best practices for Zoom Events [7][8][3].
- Riverside: 2026 tutorial; records in 4K and includes Magic Clips for post-event content creation [6].
- Minimal-setup exemplar: 13:55 YouTube tutorial published 2026‑03‑19 on Live Production Tips & Tools channel [2].
- Planning: 2026 webinar planning guide (dated November 28, 2025) foregrounds coordination and promotion checklists [5].

## Gaps / Caveats
- No validated benchmarks in these sources for session length, “best” day/time, or average drop-off patterns; treat widely repeated figures as unverified within this corpus [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].
- Reminder/registration sequences: platform invitation exists (Zoom shows inviting participants), and planning/promotion are emphasized, but the sources do not provide a tested cadence or copy framework for reminders [7][5].
- CTA overlays: EasyWebinar names timed CTA overlays as a core mechanic, but cross-platform implementation details (e.g., whether Zoom/WebinarJam/Riverside support native timed overlays) are not documented in the provided materials; treat the overlay as a principle unless your platform explicitly supports it [4][1][7][6].
- Post-event exports on non-Riverside platforms: the sources here do not document export workflows for Zoom/WebinarJam; only Riverside’s recording/repurposing features are specifically named [6].
